strengths: Novel and theoretically grounded combination of the Adjoint Matching stochastic-control framework with weak-form PDE residuals to fine-tune flow-matching models, extended to jointly evolve a latent parameter field alongside the state — this addresses the practically important setting where paired parameter-state training data is unavailable.

The use of weak-form (rather than strong-form) residuals via randomly sampled compactly-supported Wendland test functions is a sensible and numerically stable design choice, well justified via integration-by-parts derivations for both PDE systems studied.

Broad set of experimental settings (denoising of noisy observations, sparse-observation guidance, 3D super-resolution with boundary constraints, and misspecified boundary conditions) demonstrates the flexibility of the framework.

The proposed running-cost regularizer (λf) that anchors the fine-tuned parameter trajectory to the base-model's inferred parameter is a useful practical mechanism to prevent mode collapse/diversity loss during fine-tuning, and its effect is clearly illustrated (Fig. 2, Table 2).
Reasonably detailed appendices (datasets, architecture, training algorithm, hyperparameters) support reproducibility, and the authors state code/data release.
weaknesses: Experimental validation is narrow: only two canonical, synthetic PDE systems (Darcy flow and a linear acoustic wave equation) at modest resolution, with no real observational data or more complex/coupled/nonlinear PDEs, despite the paper's stated motivation of scientific inverse problems in atmospheric/seismic/medical domains.

Quantitative comparison to prior physics-constrained generative baselines is very limited — despite an extensive related-work section citing PBFM (Baldan et al. 2025), Bastek et al. (2024), DiffusionPDE (Huang et al. 2024), PhyDA, Utkarsh et al. (2025), etc., the only empirical baseline comparison is a single qualitative comparison to ECI (Cheng et al. 2024) in the appendix, with no quantitative metrics reported for it.

Evaluation relies heavily on qualitative visual figures and small sample counts (128–256 samples) for quantitative tables; no confidence intervals/repeated seeds are reported for the main comparisons, and no standard generative-quality metrics (e.g., FID or similar) are used alongside the custom pointwise statistics.

The method has many interacting hyperparameters (λx, λα, λf, test-function scale ranges, tail-refinement schedule, loss clipping thresholds) and the paper shows the method is fairly sensitive to these choices (e.g., mode collapse without regularization, need for careful λx tuning in the misspecification experiment), raising concerns about robustness and ease of practical use.

The authors explicitly characterize the experiments as "preliminary" in the conclusion, and no ablation is provided to justify the necessity of the more complex joint vector-field evolution of α over the simpler push-forward-through-φ baseline mentioned in the method section.

Scalability is a concern: the 3D super-resolution experiment requires ~12 hours of fine-tuning on a single GPU for a relatively small case, and no discussion of scaling behavior to larger/more realistic 3D or multi-physics systems is provided.

The comparison with ECI is acknowledged by the authors themselves to be somewhat unfair (gradient-free vs. gradient-based, no PDE awareness), weakening the strength of this sole empirical baseline comparison.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: enforcing parameter-dependent PDE constraints in generative models without requiring paired solution-parameter training data, which is important for realistic scientific inverse problems.

Solid theoretical extension of the Adjoint Matching framework (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025), including a well-justified scaled memoryless noise schedule (Lemma 1) that provides a practical stabilization/exploration knob.

The joint evolution of state and latent parameter via a surrogate base flow derived from an inverse predictor is a clean and reasonably novel architectural idea that enables amortized parameter inference during fine-tuning.

Extensive empirical evaluation across four distinct PDE families (Darcy, elasticity, Helmholtz, Stokes) plus a natural-image application, with sensible baselines (vanilla FM, PBFM, ECI, ablations Base AM/Base AM+φ) and multiple complementary metrics (weak/strong residuals, MMD_x, MMD_α, SSIM diversity).

Careful and honest experimental design: deliberately introduces model misspecification (BC changes, damping mismatch, missing forcing) to test robustness, which is a meaningful and more realistic stress test than typical in-distribution physics-constrained generation papers.

Strong reproducibility effort: detailed appendices with full architecture specs, hyperparameters, weak-residual derivations (with integration-by-parts) for each PDE, and full training algorithm (Algorithm 1).
Ablations (Fig. 3, 5, 9-11, 13) clearly illustrate controllable trade-offs between residual reduction, distributional fidelity, and sample diversity, giving practitioners actionable guidance.
Cross-domain demonstration on natural images (parametric recoloring + PickScore) shows the framework generalizes beyond PDE settings, strengthening the generality claim.
weaknesses: The method has many interacting components (weak residuals, joint flow, regularization term f(α), scaled noise schedule, correction heads) making it difficult to cleanly attribute gains to individual design choices; while ablations exist, the overall system is complex and could be hard to reproduce/tune in practice.

All PDE experiments use small, synthetic, low-resolution (64x64) 2D benchmarks with simple two-phase or Gaussian-random-field coefficient structures; it remains unclear how the method scales to higher-dimensional, more realistic, or real observational scientific data.

Several quantitative results show large error bars/overlapping confidence intervals across methods and hyperparameters (e.g., Table 2, Table 13), raising questions about the statistical robustness of some comparative claims (e.g., Helmholtz AM vs Base AM improvements are often within one standard deviation).

For the Stokes experiment, weak/strong residuals are comparable across ablations and the main advantage of the joint model is confined to MMD_α, a relatively narrow win that is not strongly emphasized as a limitation in the main text.

The PBFM baseline is arguably placed at an structural disadvantage since it is a training-time method evaluated under deliberately introduced misspecification; while the authors acknowledge this, it complicates fair comparison and interpretation of the reported gains over PBFM.

Core theoretical contribution (adjoint matching for reward tilting) is inherited from prior work; the paper's main novelty—joint state-parameter evolution via a surrogate base flow and residual correction heads—is somewhat incremental from an architectural standpoint (essentially conditioning/augmenting existing backbones).

No real-world (non-synthetic) scientific dataset or downstream task (e.g., actual sensor data, benchmark inverse problems used in the PINN/data-assimilation literature) is used to validate practical utility, limiting evidence for real-world impact.

The natural-image experiment, while interesting, is a fairly different problem (parametric recoloring is not a genuine physical/PDE constraint) and its connection to the main physics-constrained narrative feels somewhat tangential and under-analyzed quantitatively (only qualitative images shown, no numeric reward/diversity trade-off table).
